content: Dental cavities, also known as caries, are structural damage or holes that form in the teeth. Here is a detailed explanation of the topic: Symptoms of Dental Cavities In some cases, there may be no symptoms at all. When symptoms are present, they can include: Tooth pain or an aching sensation, especially after consuming sweet, hot, or cold foods and beverages. Visible pits or holes in the teeth. Causes of Dental Cavities Tooth decay is one of the most common disorders, second only to the common cold. Bacteria naturally reside in the mouth. These bacteria convert all types of food, particularly sugars and starches, into acids. A combination of bacteria, acids, food debris, and saliva forms a sticky substance called plaque, which adheres to the teeth. Plaque is most prominent on the back molars, just above the gum line on all teeth, and at the edges of fillings. If plaque is not removed, it mineralizes into tartar. Both plaque and tartar irritate the gums, leading to gingivitis and eventually periodontitis. Plaque begins to accumulate on teeth within 20 minutes after eating, which is when bacterial activity is at its peak. If plaque is not thoroughly and routinely removed, tooth decay will not only begin but also progress. The acids in plaque dissolve the enamel surface of the tooth, creating cavities. Cavities are typically painless until they become large enough to affect the nerves or cause a tooth fracture. If left untreated, a tooth abscess can develop. Untreated decay can also destroy the internal structures of the tooth (pulp) and ultimately lead to tooth loss. Risk Factors Cavities are more common in children and young adults but can affect individuals of any age. They are a frequent cause of tooth loss in younger people. Diets high in carbohydrates (sugars and starches) increase the risk of tooth decay.
